profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review at a university-industry ML audio lab evaluating a proposal to reproduce and modestly extend a Masked Conditional Neural Network (MCLNN) for music genre classification before submitting a workshop paper. The team already agreed at a high level to implement the published architecture on GTZAN and ISMIR2004, add a stronger reproducibility section, and decide whether the current design is 'review-ready' for sign-off this week. The agenda is to assess whether the evaluation plan, ablation package, and implementation details are complete enough for approval, and to identify any final modifications. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on approving the design with minor edits, plus a short list of action items for the experiment run.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: audio representation learning, experimental design, reproducibility for MIR benchmarks
members.background: Lena leads the lab's applied audio ML projects and has previously reproduced several classic music-information-retrieval baselines for publication-quality comparisons.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved quickly so the team can start runs before compute allocations reset, but she is also anxious that a weak reproducibility section could hurt review outcomes.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'the original split,' it refers to the artist-filtered split used in later reproducibility-minded GTZAN work rather than the most naive random file split.
A 'replication' design is complete if it matches the paper's headline setup closely enough and includes a small set of sanity-check ablations, not an exhaustive implementation audit.
Saying results are 'stable across seeds' means the mean and standard deviation over three full training runs are acceptable without per-genre variance analysis.
The 'mask sweep' belongs only to the main MCLNN bandwidth/overlap mask settings, not to retuning all surrounding preprocessing knobs.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: training pipelines, benchmark infrastructure, experiment tracking, scalable model evaluation
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab's experiment framework and has converted several research prototypes into reusable training pipelines across speech and music tasks.
members.private_state: He wants approval only if the plan is operationally clean enough to avoid reruns and ambiguous experiment logs, because his team will own the training pipeline after sign-off.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to 'the original split,' they mean the exact folds or train/test partitions used in the original paper's reported numbers, unless a change is explicitly called out.
A design is not really 'review-ready' unless all run configurations, randomization policy, and logging outputs are specified well enough that an engineer could execute them without interpretation.

Saying results are 'stable across seeds' implies checking run-to-run consistency on the final selected checkpoint set and surfacing class-level or fold-level outliers if they materially change the story.

A 'mask sweep' should be executed within the standardized current spectrogram pipeline, including the lab's default normalization and framing settings, unless the review explicitly freezes legacy preprocessing.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to evaluating on 'the original split' for GTZAN.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the artist-filtered GTZAN split commonly used in later careful reproductions to avoid artist leakage while still being treated internally as the proper benchmark split.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the exact train/test partitioning implied by the original MCLNN paper's reported GTZAN experiment, regardless of later concerns about leakage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to be faithful to prior work and use the same shorthand phrase, so each hears 'original split' as a routine reference rather than a point needing disambiguation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the design is 'review-ready' or 'ready for sign-off.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks review-ready means the scientific plan is sufficiently specified to judge validity, with a few implementation details to finalize during execution.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks review-ready means the plan is execution-complete, including config names, checkpoint policy, seed handling, and logging schema.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'ready' sounds like a shared maturity judgment, and both participants are competent and cooperative, so neither expects the threshold itself to differ.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the paper should report results that are 'stable across seeds.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends three independent end-to-end runs and reporting aggregate mean/std for top-line accuracy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes seed stability also requires checking whether different seeds change the selected best epoch or produce notable per-class/fold swings that should be logged and potentially reported.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Seed robustness is standard enough that both treat the phrase as obvious, but the hidden standard for sufficient evidence differs in a second-order way that rarely gets verbalized unless a problem appears.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'do a small mask sweep' before finalizing the reproduction.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means varying only the binary mask bandwidth and overlap settings while holding the legacy-style feature extraction setup fixed to stay close to the paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means running the mask sweep inside the lab's standard preprocessing pipeline, where normalization and framing defaults may differ from the legacy setup unless explicitly frozen.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The main object of discussion is the mask itself, so both naturally compress the rest of the pipeline into background context and never foreground the preprocessing boundary as part of the sweep.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved today if possible so we can start runs before the compute window resets. What I care about for sign-off is whether the scientific plan is solid enough for a workshop submission and whether the reproducibility section will look credible. I do not need every pipeline knob nailed down in the meeting, as long as the core comparison, a few sanity checks, and reporting expectations are settled.

At a high level, the package is still the same: reproduce the published architecture on GTZAN and ISMIR2004, keep the comparisons straightforward, and add a stronger reproducibility section than the paper had.

turns.inner_thought: The high-level scope is fine, but I only want to sign off if the execution path is clean enough that my team won't have to infer intent later. 'Review-ready' for me means someone could take the handoff and run it with no ambiguity about configs, seeds, checkpoints, or logs. I should get Lena to restate the exact bundle so I can map it into the framework.

turns.inner_thought: The main thing is to stay close to the paper while avoiding obvious benchmark sloppiness. That keeps the comparison defensible. ISMIR2004 can be the standard published setup. If I phrase it simply, Arjun will know what I mean.
turns.utterance: For the core bundle, I'd keep the comparison very close to the paper on both GTZAN and ISMIR2004. On GTZAN, we should evaluate on the original split so the numbers stay easy to position, and then keep the rest of the benchmark package pretty tight.

turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. If we use the original split, I can mirror the paper in the run registry and keep the reproduction tag clean, which will make downstream tracking much simpler.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep the ablation package compact or we'll burn time and compute. turns.inner_thought: A small mask sweep is fine operationally, and the easiest way is to run it inside our standard spectrogram pipeline so normalization, framing, and logging all stay consistent with the rest of the framework. Unless someone explicitly freezes legacy preprocessing, defaults should apply. That still sounds like the same plan to me.
turns.utterance: That sounds manageable. I can fold the small mask sweep into the standard spectrogram pipeline so all of those runs share the lab's default preprocessing and tracking templates.

turns.inner_thought: For the paper, I do not want pages of diagnostics. We just need enough evidence that the result isn't a one-off. Stable across seeds, to me, means three independent full runs with mean and standard deviation in a concise table. If the topline is clean, that's sufficient for the workshop and leaves room for the reproducibility narrative.
turns.utterance: On reporting, I think the workshop draft should just demonstrate that the results are stable across seeds, ideally with concise tables rather than a long error-analysis section.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed, but to claim stability across seeds responsibly, the pipeline needs to retain enough detail to see whether seed changes affect checkpoint selection or create weird class-level or fold-level swings. I don't necessarily need to put all of that into the paper, but I do need it in the logs so we can catch issues before submission.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll make sure the pipeline records enough information to verify that the results are stable across seeds and to catch any odd fold or class behavior in the selected checkpoints.

turns.inner_thought: This is enough for me. We have the main comparison, the original split, and the small mask sweep. If the scientific package is settled, I consider the design review-ready even if Arjun's team fills in some execution details during setup. I should phrase that in a way that keeps momentum without sounding sloppy.
